instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 271 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 105.2, target 72.2. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 14.4, target 16.7. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 30.1, target 24.0. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 3.2, target 2.8. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 2.2. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 3.1, target 8.5. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 21.2, target -8.5. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 0.9, target 0.9. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I am writing to urge you to adopt Policy 1, which allows students to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, provided they are switched off during class. A total ban may seem like the simpler choice, but it would cost students more than it protects.

First, phones are part of how students stay safe. Many families rely on them to confirm pickup times, check in after a bus is late, or reach a parent during an emergency. Under Policy 2, those students would have no reliable way to reach home during the school day.

Second, a ban treats students as if they cannot manage a simple rule. Policy 1 already sets a clear boundary: phones stay off during class. Students who respect that boundary keep their phones; those who break it can lose the privilege. This teaches responsibility, which students will need long after they leave school.

Third, free time matters. Lunch and passing periods are when students eat, talk with friends, and decompress. A phone is often how they read the news, reply to a family message, or simply take a break from the crowd. Removing that option does not make those minutes more productive. It only makes them more crowded.

Finally, enforcing a full ban would demand constant monitoring, lockers, and confiscations, all of which take staff time away from students. Policy 1 is easier to supervise because the rule is simple and visible.

I respectfully ask you to choose Policy 1. It keeps students connected, builds responsibility, and gives them reasonable freedom within clear limits.

Respectfully,
A Concerned Student
